newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT SLAMMED.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT SLAMMED.

text.p: Auditor-General Henri Kleuver on Wednesday reported a further deterioration in financial management in South African government departments and called for urgent corrective measures.

Presenting his report on the 1995/96 government accounts to parliament, Kleuver said that this applied to both how government spent and collected money, although he hoped that the new South African Revenue Service would improve revenue collection dramtically.
He said his report was more comprehensive this year because of more comprehensive audits.
"But, on the other hand, it is clear that the quality of financial management and administration in many institutions has deteriorated," he said.

Kleuver blamed this on the exodus of skilled staff members who had taken advantage of the voluntary retrenchment packages offered as part of the restructuring of the civil service to include more black staff.
Deputy Auditor-General Bertie Loots said the problem had been compounded by the introduction of a new basic accounting system that had "not delivered what it was supposed to deliver."
Director General of State Expenditure Hannes Smit said there was no easy solution to the lack of skilled staff but extensive training programmes had been launched.
He said the new accounting system had not worked because it had been introduced on different computer systems instead of being linked to one mainframe computer. This was being rectified.
"We have been through a rough patch with the basic accounting system but we think we will have it under control next year."

Kleuver said he was unable to issue unqualified audits for 22 departments and had come across unauthorised expenditure totalling 151.6 million rand in nine departments, the largest of which was by the health department at 58 million rand.
He said that unauthorised expenditure did necessarily not imply fraud or corruption, but usually that accounting officers had not followed the correct procedures.
A common fault had been not following tender board directives when buying goods or services and employing consultants.
Local governments continued to experience serious cash flow problems and often did not have enough funds to pay for electricity bought from Eskom or salaries for staff.
Customs and excise had continued to exercise poor control over imports and exports and irregularities were rife. Pending legislation to give the revenue service full autonomy was now urgently needed.
